title: The Lesson I Learned When Thomas Needed to See Before Believing
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned When Thomas Needed to See Before Believing
(John 20:25)
Thomas gets judged too quickly.

We call him doubting.
Jesus called him back.
That hit me hard.

Because if I’m honest, I’ve had Thomas moments. Moments when pain was louder than promise. Moments when I said, “Lord, unless I see You move, unless I touch the proof, unless You answer this the way I expect… I can’t believe.”

That is where Thomas was in John 20:25. The other disciples were celebrating resurrection, but Thomas was still bleeding from Friday. He had watched hope get nailed to a cross. He had seen the horror. So when they said, “We have seen the Lord,” Thomas answered from wounded logic: “Unless I see… I will not believe.”
And here’s the lesson.

Sometimes unbelief is not rebellion.
Sometimes it is heartbreak wearing armor.

But here’s what we miss: Jesus did not abandon Thomas in his struggle. Eight days later, Christ came back for the one man who couldn’t get there yet. He stepped into the room, into the fear, into the doubt, and offered the very evidence Thomas demanded.
That wrecks me.
Because Jesus is not scared of honest wrestlings. He is holy, yes. He is risen, yes. But He is also merciful. He does not always crush the doubter. He calls him closer.

Still, the story does not glorify doubt. It exposes it. Thomas had to learn what we all must learn: faith cannot live forever on visible proof. Sooner or later, we must trust the Word of the risen Christ. We must bow, not because we have controlled the evidence, but because He is Lord.
And when Thomas finally saw Jesus, he didn’t just say, “Now I get it.”
He said, “My Lord and my God.”

That is the goal.
Not just answers.
Surrender.
Thomas teaches me that Jesus can handle my questions, but He will not leave me in them. He comes near, reveals Himself, and leads me from hesitation to worship.
And that points us straight to the Gospel.

Because the risen Jesus still comes for wounded sinners, skeptical hearts, and shame-filled souls. He comes with nail-scarred hands. He comes with peace. He comes not just to prove He is alive, but to save all who will believe in Him. We are not redeemed by having perfect faith. We are redeemed by a perfect Savior.
So when your heart says, “I need to see first,” remember this: the cross is already proof of His love, and the empty tomb is already proof of His power.

You may be struggling.
You may be doubting.
You may be tired.

But don’t run from Jesus in your questions.
Run to Him.
